title: Iran Offered to Reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump Said No.
summary:
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman — and a huge share of the world's oil travels through it. Iran effectively closed the strait after the U.S. and Israel attacked it in late February, and ship traffic has dropped sharply because of Iranian threats and attacks on vessels.

This week, Iran made an offer: reopen the strait and resume talks on its nuclear program in seven days, if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales, and observes a ceasefire that would include Lebanon. On Saturday, President Donald Trump rejected it. "They want to make a deal and I think that's fine," Trump told reporters outside the White House before leaving for a college football game. "I'd like to make a deal, too. But that deal would not be acceptable." He said Iran was "losing so badly."

Before rejecting the proposal, Trump posted an image on his Truth Social platform of the Strait of Hormuz labeled "Trump Strait." It is not the first time he has tried to antagonize Iran in this way.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had just left New York after the annual United Nations gathering of world leaders, where Iran held indirect talks with the U.S. In his U.N. speech, Pezeshkian pushed back against Trump's threat to "annihilate" Iran, but ended by saying Tehran remains open to diplomacy. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, described the seven-day proposal to journalists Friday night.

Pezeshkian also told CBS that, from his viewpoint as a physician, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has "no specific ongoing health issues" despite not being seen or heard in public since the war began in February. The interview will air Sunday. Pezeshkian said his most recent meeting with Khamenei lasted over seven hours. "From a medical standpoint, he's completely healthy," the president said.

Separately, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile it blames on Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, fired toward the city of Khamis Mushait. Military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki claimed the interception early Saturday. The Associated Press could not independently verify the claim. The Gulf Cooperation Council condemned the attacks as a "grave escalation and threat to regional security." Iraq said it is talking with the U.S. about exemptions from sanctions on Iranian airlines.
why_it_matters: A narrow stretch of water between Iran and Oman partly decides what families around the world pay for fuel, food and travel, so a standoff there can raise prices far away from the Middle East and make war more likely.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea passage between the Persian Gulf and the open ocean, squeezed between Iran and Oman. A large share of the oil traded by sea travels through it, so any threat to close it makes energy prices jump around the world.

It has been a flashpoint before: during the Iran–Iraq war, both sides attacked oil tankers in the Gulf, and the U.S. Navy escorted Kuwaiti tankers to keep shipping safe. Iran has also threatened to shut the strait during earlier standoffs over its nuclear program, which world powers have negotiated about for years — a past agreement limited Iran's nuclear work in return for relief from sanctions, but the United States later pulled out of it.

The Houthi rebels (an armed group in Yemen that fights the country's government and is backed by Iran) have fired missiles at Saudi Arabia before. Saudi Arabia and Iran are regional rivals, and the Gulf Cooperation Council (a group of Gulf Arab states that coordinates security and economic policy) speaks for them on such attacks.

The United Nations (where almost every country meets each year to discuss world problems) hosted the talks mentioned in the article. Iran's Supreme Leader (the country's highest authority, who has the final say on major decisions) has not been seen or heard in public since the war began in February.

OPEN QUESTION: Can any deal be reached — and what happens to oil and shipping if the strait stays shut?

perspectives.description: Iran's offer to reopen the strait and return to nuclear talks suggests it wants a way out of the confrontation. If a deal were reached, oil tankers could move again and prices could settle down, and a ceasefire including Lebanon could reduce fighting on several fronts at once.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the offer looks like a demand for rewards
perspectives.description: The U.S. side appears to see Iran's conditions — lifting the naval blockade, waiving oil sanctions, a wider ceasefire — as too much to give in exchange for reopening a waterway Iran itself closed. Trump's 'Trump Strait' post and his remark that Iran is 'losing so badly' suggest Washington wants pressure to keep working rather than a quick bargain.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — the strait as a bargaining chip
perspectives.description: The Strait of Hormuz has been used as leverage before: whoever controls or threatens it can affect global oil markets, so both sides have an incentive to keep it in play. Much of this round is being fought in public — Truth Social posts and U.N. speeches — as well as in private talks, which makes it hard to tell how close a deal really is.

Iran's president still says Tehran is open to diplomacy, so talks could restart with different terms, and Iraq's request for sanctions exemptions shows neighboring states are already working around the conflict. The bigger question is whether the missile exchanges and the closed strait stay contained or pull more countries in.
